podcast.title: Lyric Writing Process
podcast.body: Rupert Holmes wrote "Escape (The Piña Colada Song)" when he needed an upbeat track to balance an album of ballads. With the music already composed and being repetitive, he focused intensely on the lyrics, trying various ideas. He discarded some, like "That's the law of the jungle in the school of the street," finding them bad and sounding like a Billy Joel song. He also considered "Cruel to Be Kind" but realized Nick Lowe already had a song with that title. "He had the music already, which is quite repetitive, so he needed the lyrics to be the focal point."

podcast.title: Multi-Talented Artist
podcast.body: Rupert Holmes is most remembered for "Escape (The Piña Colada Song)," though he also has a distinguished career in musical theatre, having written the musical "The Mystery of Edwin Drood" for which he won Emmys and Tonys. He has also written a novel that was adapted into a movie. Despite these accomplishments, he remains predominantly identified with his most famous song. "He for example also wrote the musical, The Mystery of Edwin Druid, He's One Emmys, He's One Tonys, He's written a novel that was made into a movie, but he will always be the Pina Colada Song Guy."

podcast.title: Personal Ad Inspiration
podcast.body: The inspiration for the lyrics of "Escape (The Piña Colada Song)" came from a copy of The Village Voice and its personal ads, which happened to be lying nearby. Rupert Holmes wondered what would happen if he answered one of these ads, immediately thinking it would probably turn out to be his own wife. This spontaneous thought became the core narrative of the song. "As sometimes happens with writers, he was inspired by something that just happened to be laying nearby. In this case, it was a copy of the village voice and the personal ads."

podcast.title: Song Title Evolution
podcast.body: The song "Escape (The Piña Colada Song)" was originally just titled "Escape." However, due to popular demand and the way people requested it in record shops, it was officially retitled to "The Piña Colada Song" to match how the public identified it. "The song was originally just called Escape, but when people went into the record shops to request the Pina Colada Song, and there was no record called the Pina Colada Song, the logic dictates that you make it the Pina Colada Song."

podcast.title: Vocal Delivery as Key to Success
podcast.body: Rupert Holmes's singing voice, described as "not that great," was considered a crucial element in the success of "Escape (The Piña Colada Song)." It made him sound like an ordinary person who would respond to a personal ad and contemplate cheating on his partner, lending authenticity to the song's narrative that a more polished singer, like Neil Diamond, might not have achieved. "I mean, if somebody with real pipes sang this, like if Neil Diamond sang it, it just wouldn't work. But Holmes sounds like a guy who would respond to a personal ad and cheat on his old lady rather than just breaking it off with her."
